design_detail: Critical review with a stated search (PubMed, Google Scholar, Embase; studies published 1999–2016) of human studies comparing people with a history of cocaine use with non-drug-using controls on cognitive tests, either alone (Table 1, 22 studies) or with brain imaging (Table 2, 25 studies: 6 MRI, 14 fMRI, 3 PET, 2 EEG, editors' count of rows), each tabulated with the reviewers' caveats (normative comparison, matching on age and education, control of other drug use, number of measures, sample size). No quantitative synthesis; a short section on animal studies. Read from the accepted manuscript, not the version of record.
can_establish: Which methodological safeguards (comparison with norms, demographic matching, control of other drug use, more than one measure per domain, verified abstinence) were missing from the tabulated studies as the reviewers judged them, and that many imaging studies reported brain differences without a group difference on the cognitive task they used.
cannot_establish: Whether long-term cocaine use does or does not cause cognitive deficits (nothing is pooled, every tabulated human study is cross-sectional, and by the reviewers' own account most are confounded and unnormed); what proportion of measures showed differences (never counted); or that the tabulated studies are the relevant literature (no record of selection, no list of exclusions, and many studies tabulated by Spronk et al., 2013, are absent).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review). Search of PubMed, Google Scholar and Embase with terms combining cocaine with cognition, cognitive functioning, cognitive deficits and cognitive impairment, limited to human laboratory studies; search dates, numbers retrieved and screened, the selection procedure and reasons for exclusion are not reported (§2 Methods, PDF p. 5).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Studies of long-term effects published 1999–2016 comparing people with a history of recreational use, abuse or dependence with non-drug-using controls, using neuropsychological tests, MRI, fMRI, PET or EEG; abstinence defined as at least 72 hours without cocaine; groups of 18 or fewer flagged as small (§2 Methods, PDF p. 5). The tables nonetheless include a study without a control group, a study comparing treatment completers with non-completers, and several studies testing people within 72 hours of use or with cocaine-positive urine (see reporting issues).
sample.demographics: Not summarized. Tables 1–2 give group sizes and diagnoses (DSM-III or DSM-IV dependence or abuse, or recreational use), with age and education differences mentioned only in the caveats.
sample.selection_effects: Selection is undocumented. Editors' cross-check: about 30 long-term studies tabulated by Spronk et al. (2013, Table 3), all within this review's date range, do not appear in Tables 1–2, including van der Plas et al. (2009), which this review's own introduction cites as replicating a WCST impairment; whether they were excluded or missed cannot be told. The tabulated samples are mostly people with cocaine dependence recruited for research or treatment, with some recreational samples (Colzato, Hulka, Preller, Reske, Sellaro, Soar, Vonmoos).

exposure.measurement: Varies across tabulated studies: DSM-III or DSM-IV diagnosis or self-described recreational use; urine toxicology in some, self-report only in others (flagged, for example, for Cunha, Oliveira, Sellaro, Soar, Morein-Zamir and the social-gaze fMRI study of Preller); hair toxicology in Vonmoos et al. (2013) (Tables 1–2, PDF pp. 26–39).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not extracted by the review: the tables have no columns for amount, frequency, duration or route of use.
exposure.polysubstance: Flagged study by study in the caveats and counted in the text (other drug use not controlled in 8 of 22 neuropsychological studies, 8 of 14 fMRI studies and 5 of 6 MRI studies; PDF pp. 8, 10–11); not analysed. The reviewers note that one MRI sample included people dependent on nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and heroin (Ersche et al., 2011; PDF p. 11).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Defined as at least 72 hours, but Tables 1–2 include studies with shorter or unknown abstinence or cocaine-positive urine at testing or screening (editors' count: at least 8 of 22 neuropsychological and 7 of 25 imaging studies; unknown for 6 more).

comparison.controls: Non-drug-using controls in most tabulated studies; some controls used alcohol, cannabis or MDMA (Sellaro et al., 2013; drug use in the control group of the Preller social-gaze fMRI study); further comparison groups with pathological gambling (Albein-Urios et al., 2012), alcohol dependence (Goldstein et al., 2004) and methamphetamine use (Simon et al.); one fMRI study had no control group (Goldstein et al., 2007) and one study compared treatment completers with non-completers only (Streeter et al., 2008).
comparison.matching: Per the reviewers: 5 of 22 neuropsychological studies not matched on age and 6 not matched on education; in several imaging studies groups with cocaine use disorder around 40 years old were compared with controls around 30 (PDF pp. 8, 14).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No tabulated human study measured cognition before cocaine use; the reviewers propose demographically adjusted norms as the reference instead (§5 Discussion, 5th paragraph, PDF p. 15).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Sometimes present and flagged in the caveats; not systematically reported.

outcomes.instruments: Wide range across studies: Stroop, Go/No-Go, stop-signal task, WCST, Iowa Gambling Task, delay discounting, CVLT, RAVLT, n-back, digit span, CANTAB tests, Trail Making, DSST, social-cognition tasks; structural MRI (voxel-based morphometry), task fMRI, FDG-PET and EEG event-related potentials (Tables 1–2).
outcomes.validity_norms: The review's central argument: individual performance should be judged against demographically adjusted norms (for example T scores below 40, or cut-offs of 1, 1.5 or 2 SD below the normative mean), not only against a control group (PDF pp. 3, 15).
outcomes.operationalization: For the reviewers, impairment requires performance below demographically adjusted norms, ideally on more than one measure per domain, with age, education, sex and other drug use matched or controlled; a statistically significant group difference is not by itself impairment (PDF pp. 8, 14–15).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis); the review does not count measures across studies.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable to the review; not extracted for the primary studies.

analysis.effect_sizes: None computed or pooled. The review reports tallies of study features: of 22 neuropsychological studies, 3 with more than one measure per domain, 5 not age-matched, 6 not education-matched, 8 not controlling for other drug use, 13 without normative interpretation (PDF p. 8); of 14 fMRI studies, 8 with a single measure, 8 not controlling for other drug use, 11 without a cognitive group difference (PDF pp. 11–12); of 6 MRI studies, 3 drawing behavioural conclusions without cognitive testing, 2 not controlling for age, 5 not controlling for other drug use (PDF p. 10); of 3 PET studies, 2 not age-matched and 2 without a cognitive group difference (PDF p. 13). Editors' count from Table 1: 19 of the 21 studies with a non-drug-using control group list poorer performance of a cocaine group in at least one domain.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: No record of selection or exclusions; several of the text's tallies disagree with the entries of Table 1; the abstract's statement that differences were found on a minority of measures rests on no count reported anywhere in the paper.
analysis.power: The reviewers flag groups of 18 or fewer as small, from a power calculation for d = 0.74 giving 18.8 per group for 80% power and 25.3 for 90% (PDF p. 5). Editors' calculation (two-sided two-sample t-test, α = .05, noncentral t): d = 0.74 needs 30 per group for 80% power and 40 for 90%; 18 per group gives about 58% power.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 47 tabulated studies, most neuropsychological studies list poorer performance of a cocaine group than controls in at least one domain (editors' count 19 of 21 with controls), and the reviewers themselves say differences are most consistent in executive function and working or verbal memory; most imaging studies report brain differences, while 11 of 14 fMRI and 2 of 3 PET studies found no group difference on their, often single, cognitive task. Most studies lacked normative comparison, demographic matching or control of other drug use; in the two studies whose caveats mention norms, performance was within the normative range, and the one PET study using age-adjusted scores found mild impairment (less than 1 SD below the control mean).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and highlights state that “differences in cognitive performance were observed on a minority of measures” (PDF pp. 2–3), a proportion the paper never counts, and conclude that the evidence does not support broad deficits and that the view that people who use cocaine have broad deficits is inaccurate and may harm treatment and policy (PDF pp. 3, 16). The tabulated studies can show that impairment has not been demonstrated to the reviewers' standard, but not that deficits are absent: the same confounding and lack of norms that undermine claims of impairment also undermine a claim of no impairment, and the highlights concede that the strongest evidence of harm concerns executive functions (PDF p. 2). The animal section, declared outside the review's scope, ends with a firm statement that preclinical research does not support neurotoxicity or permanent prefrontal change (PDF p. 7).

timeline.event: Quantitative review of studies from 1987–2002 (Jovanovski et al.), cited by this review as covering the earlier period
Review with meta-analyses of 2003–2013 studies (Spronk et al.) concluding that long-term use goes with a general cognitive impairment; this review quotes that conclusion and disputes it
Systematic quantitative review of cocaine and cognition including abstinence duration (Potvin et al., 2014, as cited in this review; not read)
This review: 22 neuropsychological and 25 imaging studies tabulated with caveats; no pooling
Systematic review and meta-analysis of cocaine use and cognitive inhibition (López-Martín et al.; appraised separately)

replication.where_it_stands: Spronk et al. (2013) and this review read largely overlapping cross-sectional evidence in opposite directions: the first pools group differences and calls them general impairment, the second stresses missing norms, matching and control of other drugs and calls the impairment view inaccurate. Both readings go beyond the data. Poorer average performance of people with cocaine dependence than controls in executive function and memory is consistently reported; its cause, its persistence with abstinence and its clinical meaning remain unsettled.

funding.funder: Not reported (no funding statement in the accepted manuscript).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no financial interests and no conflicts of interest (Declarations of interest, PDF p. 16).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychology, Columbia University (Frazer, Richards) and Department of Psychiatry, University of Vermont Medical Center (Keith). None of the tabulated studies is by the review's authors. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A pre-registered systematic review with a documented search and selection, study-level risk-of-bias assessment and a quantitative synthesis that scores each study against demographically adjusted norms (the proportion of each group below a stated cut-off, as well as group differences), with moderator analyses by verified abstinence, alcohol and other drug use, education and recreational versus dependent use; and prospective cohorts that test cognition before regular cocaine use and repeatedly during biologically verified abstinence.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (people with a history of recreational use, abuse or dependence, abstinent at least 72 hours), exposure, comparator (non-drug-using controls) and outcomes (cognition and neuroimaging) are stated (PDF p. 5).
No protocol or registration is mentioned.

The reviewers explain that ethical limits on giving cocaine to people without prior use leave comparisons of abstinent people with controls as the available design (Introduction, 4th paragraph, PDF p. 4).

Three sources with search terms, and a date range justified by earlier reviews (PDF p. 5); but no search date, no full strategy, Google Scholar as a main source, no reference-list or grey-literature searching and no language statement. About 30 studies tabulated by Spronk et al. (2013) within the date range are absent, which suggests the search or selection was incomplete.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No list of excluded studies and no flow of records.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Tables 1–2 give domains and tests, group sizes and diagnoses, abstinence, direction of findings and caveats (PDF pp. 26–39), but no amounts or frequency of use, ages, education values or recruitment settings.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: The caveats column addresses confounding (age, education, other drug use, psychiatric comorbidity) for most studies and some selection and exposure-measurement problems, but without a stated tool or criteria, unevenly, and with text tallies that disagree with the table. A close call between partial yes and no; the overall rating does not depend on it.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The interpretation is built around the studies' confounding, lack of norms and single measures (PDF pp. 8, 10–15), although this is used to dismiss impairment rather than to grade it.
Conflicting results between studies are discussed and attributed to differences in age, education, other drug use, single measures and inpatient housing (for example PDF pp. 11–14).
No quantitative synthesis; the reviewers note in passing that selecting only significant comparisons overstates estimates (PDF p. 14).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: The authors declare no financial interests or conflicts (PDF p. 16); funding of the review is not stated.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Two critical items are not met (no protocol; no list of excluded studies) and two are met only in part (search; informal risk-of-bias appraisal without a tool), which gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2; the meta-analysis items do not apply. The review's value lies in its study-by-study caveats and its argument that group differences need normative benchmarks and control of confounding; it may be cited for that argument and, with each point checked in the primary paper, for specific methodological weaknesses and for imaging studies that found brain differences without cognitive differences. It may not be cited as evidence that cocaine use leaves cognition unimpaired: its own Table 1 lists poorer performance of a cocaine group in at least one domain in most studies, its tallies disagree with its tables, its selection is undocumented and visibly incomplete, and its tables include studies that breach its own abstinence and control-group criteria.

key_findings.finding: Search and inclusion: PubMed, Google Scholar and Embase searched with terms combining cocaine with cognition, cognitive functioning, cognitive deficits and cognitive impairment, limited to human laboratory studies; studies of long-term effects published 1999–2016 comparing people with a history of recreational use, abuse or dependence with non-drug-using controls; abstinence defined as at least 72 hours without cocaine. No search dates, screening numbers, selection procedure or list of exclusions are given.

Groups of 18 or fewer were flagged as small, from an a priori power calculation for an effect of d = 0.74 (a global cognitive index from an earlier study): 18.8 per group for 80% power and 25.3 per group for 90% at a significance level of .05.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation (two-sided two-sample t-test, α = .05): d = 0.74 needs 30 per group for 80% power and 40 for 90%; 18 per group gives about 58% power.

key_findings.finding: Table 1 tabulates 22 studies using neuropsychological tests only; Table 2 tabulates imaging studies, which the text counts as six MRI, fourteen fMRI and three PET studies (two EEG studies are also listed); each row gives domains and tests, participants, abstinence, findings and the reviewers' caveats.
key_findings.locator: §4.1, 4th paragraph; §4.2, last paragraph; §4.4, 3rd paragraph; §4.5, 4th paragraph; Tables 1–2

key_findings.finding: Reviewers' tallies for the 22 neuropsychological studies: 3 used more than one measure per domain, 5 did not match groups on age, 6 did not match on education, 8 did not control for other drug use and 13 did not interpret results against norms.
key_findings.note: Only the age tally matches the caveat entries of Table 1; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Reviewers' tallies for the fourteen fMRI studies: eight used one cognitive measure per domain, eight did not control for other drug use, and eleven found no significant group difference on the cognitive measure, so their conclusions rest on the imaging alone.
Reviewers' tallies for the six MRI studies: three drew conclusions about behaviour without any cognitive testing, two did not control for age and five did not control for other drug use.
key_findings.locator: §4.2 MRI studies without cognitive testing, last paragraph

key_findings.finding: PET: of three studies, two did not match groups on age and two found no cognitive group difference while reporting regional activity differences (Bolla et al., 2003, Iowa Gambling Task after about 25 days' abstinence; Bolla et al., 2004, modified Stroop, with an older cocaine group, 36 vs 30 years, housed as inpatients longer than controls, 23 vs 3 days).
key_findings.locator: §4.5 PET studies, 2nd and 4th paragraphs (pp. 12–13); Table 2, Bolla et al. (2003) and (2004) (PET) rows (p. 38)

key_findings.finding: The one PET study that used age-adjusted test scores (Goldstein et al., 2004; 42 people with cocaine dependence, 40 with alcohol dependence, 72 controls) found mild impairment in the cocaine group, less than 1 SD below the control mean, with the alcohol group more impaired.
key_findings.locator: §4.5 PET studies, 3rd paragraph (p. 13); Table 2, Goldstein et al. (2004) (PET) row (p. 38)

key_findings.finding: In the two Table 1 studies whose caveats mention a normative comparison, performance was not outside the normative range: Reske et al. (2010), CVLT, 13 people who used cocaine recreationally vs 48 stimulant-naive controls; Woicik et al. (2011), WCST and CVLT, 107 vs 107, although the cocaine group also had poorer set-shifting and later-trial recall than controls.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Reske et al. (2010) row (p. 29) and Woicik et al. (2011) row (p. 31)
key_findings.note: The table does not say whether the primary authors or the reviewers made the normative comparison.

key_findings.finding: Editors' count from Table 1: 19 of the 21 studies with a non-drug-using control group list poorer performance of a cocaine group in at least one domain (none listed for Cunha et al. and for the Preller sensorimotor-gating study; Streeter et al., 2008, had no control group). The arrows summarize domains, not individual measures.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Cognitive findings column and legend (p. 31)

key_findings.finding: The highlights state that the strongest evidence for harmful effects concerns executive functions (attention, inhibition, working memory), and the discussion that executive function and working or verbal memory are where differences from controls have been found most consistently; the reviewers argue that a significant difference alone does not show impairment.

Confounding examples given by the reviewers: controls with more education than the cocaine group (17 vs 11.87 years in Fernández-Serrano et al.); cocaine groups older than controls (about 40 vs 30 years in four studies; 37 vs 30 years in Kaufman et al., 2003).
key_findings.locator: §4.1, 3rd paragraph (p. 8); §4.4, 2nd paragraph (p. 11); §5 Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 14); Table 2, Kaufman et al. (2003) row for the year (p. 36)

key_findings.finding: Editors' count from Tables 1–2: at least 8 of the 22 neuropsychological and 7 of the 25 imaging studies list some participants tested after less than 72 hours of abstinence or with cocaine-positive urine on the test or screening day (for example Fillmore and Rush, 2002, who required cocaine-positive urine; Vadhan et al., 2009, abstinence entered as the morning of testing; Tomasi et al., 2010, 17 of 20 urine-positive); abstinence is unknown for 6 more.

Animal evidence, kept apart from the human findings and declared outside the review's scope: the reviewers argue that rodent regimens (for example 30 mg/kg cocaine by intraperitoneal injection daily for 2 weeks in drug-naive rats) are about three times larger than the amounts people with heavy long-term use report, scaling by body weight; in rhesus monkeys self-administering cocaine, reversal-learning and working-memory deficits seen 3 days after use had normalized after 3 months of abstinence, although novel and appetitive distractors still disrupted performance in the cocaine group only, and after 20 months without cocaine there was no task difference but higher cerebellar metabolic activity.

The reviewers propose judging impairment against demographically adjusted norms, for example T scores below 40 (more than 1 SD below the normative mean) or cut-offs of 1, 1.5 or 2 SD, with groups matched or adjusted for age, education and sex.

Conclusions: the reviewers state that the evidence does not support broad cognitive deficits from chronic cocaine use, call that view inaccurate and say it may harm treatment programmes and policy; they also reject the suggestion that people with cocaine use disorder cannot benefit from cognitive behavioural therapy.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods define abstinence as at least 72 hours and the section headings describe abstinent samples, but Tables 1–2 include studies with less than 72 hours of abstinence or cocaine-positive urine (editors' count: at least 8 of 22 and 7 of 25), for example Colzato et al. (2007), 2 days; Sellaro et al. (2013), at least 2 days; Simon et al., positive on the test day; Parvaz et al. (2015), use within 72 hours.
reporting_issues.consequence: Results from people tested during recent use or early withdrawal are mixed with long-term effects, the very confound the reviewers raise for the animal studies (PDF p. 7). Two rows also differ from Spronk et al. (2013, Table 3): Colzato et al. (2007) is listed there with more than 7 days' abstinence, and Woicik et al. (2011), shown here as at least 72 hours, with under 72 hours and mostly positive urine; the caveat in this review's own Woicik row says that 19 completers tested negative for cocaine.

reporting_issues.issue: Two tabulated studies lack the non-drug-using control group the inclusion criteria require: Goldstein et al. (2007, fMRI) is marked as having no control group, and Streeter et al. (2008) compares treatment completers with non-completers.
reporting_issues.consequence: The criteria were not applied consistently; these rows cannot inform a comparison with people who do not use cocaine.

reporting_issues.issue: The text's tallies disagree with Table 1's own caveat entries: other drug use not controlled is counted as 8 studies, but the table flags at least 11 (adding Colzato 2009, Sellaro 2013 and Vonmoos 2013); education as 6, but the cited list includes reference 81, an fMRI study from Table 2, and omits two Table 1 studies the table flags (Vonmoos 2013 and the Preller sensorimotor-gating study); no normative interpretation as 13 of 22, while the table flags 11 explicitly and notes a normative comparison for two; more than one measure per domain as 3 of 22, although the same section credits Fernández-Serrano et al. with several measures per domain and Table 1 lists several tests per domain for others (for example Bolla 1999, Colzato 2009). Among the fMRI studies, the eleven counted as showing no cognitive difference include Kübler et al. (2005), which Table 2 lists with poorer visuospatial working memory.
reporting_issues.consequence: The summary counts that claims would cite cannot be relied on as printed; counts should be taken from the table rows, with their own uncertainty.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and highlights state that cognitive differences were observed on a minority of measures, but no count of measures, or of studies with and without differences, appears anywhere in the results; the editors' count from Table 1 finds poorer performance in at least one domain in 19 of 21 studies with controls.
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline result is unverifiable from the paper; at the level of studies it is contradicted by Table 1, though it may hold for the in-scanner tasks of the imaging studies (11 of 14 fMRI, 2 of 3 PET without a difference by the reviewers' count).

reporting_issues.issue: The power calculation behind the small-sample flag gives 18.8 per group for 80% power and 25.3 for 90% at d = 0.74; the editors' calculation for a two-sided two-sample comparison at α = .05 gives 30 and 40 per group.
reporting_issues.consequence: The threshold of 18 per group is lenient: studies with 19 to 29 per group are not flagged as small although they had less than 80% power for d = 0.74 (about 58% at 18 per group).

reporting_issues.issue: The comparison of animal and human exposure scales the rat dose to a 70 kg person by body weight alone, with no allometric or pharmacokinetic basis.
reporting_issues.consequence: Editors' note (METHODS §5.4): body-surface-area scaling, the usual allometric method, divides a rat mg/kg dose by about 6, which would reverse the three-fold comparison; the argument that rodent regimens far exceed human use is not established by this calculation.

reporting_issues.issue: Selection is undocumented, and the editors' cross-check shows it is incomplete: about 30 long-term studies listed by Spronk et al. (2013, Table 3), all within this review's 1999–2016 window, are not tabulated (for example Abi-Saab 2005, Kjome 2010, Lane 2007, Li 2006, Moeller 2004 and 2005, Rahman 2005, Tanabe 2009, van der Plas 2009, Verdejo-Garcia 2007, Woicik 2009), and van der Plas et al. (2009) is cited in the introduction (reference 18) as replicating a WCST impairment yet does not appear in Table 1.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison uses Spronk et al. (2013), Table 3, PDF pp. 6–9 of that review. Without an exclusion list it cannot be told whether these studies failed the criteria or were missed; conclusions about the literature as a whole rest on an unrepresentative subset of unknown selection.

reporting_issues.issue: Citation and labelling errors: five tabulated studies have no entry in the reference list (Reske 2010, Sellaro 2013, Soar 2012 and Vonmoos 2013 in Table 1; Parvaz 2015 in Table 2); table years differ from the reference list (Cuhna 2010 vs Cunha 2011; Simon 2008 vs 2001; the two Preller studies of 2013 and 2014 swapped; Castelluccio 2013 vs 2014); reference 76, cited for the Fernández-Serrano primary study, is a 2011 review (the primary study is reference 9); reference 108, cited for cocaine neurotoxicity in animals, concerns methamphetamine; references 16 and 17, cited as replications of a WCST impairment, are a theoretical perspective article and a study of self-efficacy; the same Hester and Garavan paper appears as references 4 and 102.
reporting_issues.consequence: Several primary studies cannot be traced from this review alone; identify them by DOI before citing. Some errors may have been corrected in the version of record, which was not read.

reporting_issues.issue: Internal errors in Table 2 rows: Hanlon et al. (2011) gives a mean abstinence of 1.9 days for the abstinent group and 243.8 for the current-use group, apparently transposed; Hester and Garavan (2004) gives a minimum of 72 hours with a mean of 42 hours, which cannot both be right; Gooding et al. (2008) lists poorer CPT discriminability and more commission errors but says in the caveats that no significant behavioural differences were found; Ersche et al. (2011) marks response inhibition and sustained attention with the arrow the legend reserves for better performance while describing slower responses and more missed targets.
reporting_issues.consequence: These rows should not be cited from the table; the primary papers must be read.

verification.source_read: Accepted manuscript PDF (Behavioural Brain Research, unedited, 39 PDF pages: cover page; text with running-header page numbers 1–14 on PDF pp. 2–15; references PDF pp. 15–25; Tables 1–2 PDF pp. 26–39), not the version of record (348:241–262 in the reference record), so anchors give PDF pages (PDF page = manuscript page + 1) and differ from the published pagination. All pages read; Tables 1–2 and every number on this card checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi; no figures; no supplementary material.
